# SkePU Standard Library {#sec-stdlib}

For commonly used functionality, SkePU provides a set of standard[^13]
library modules. These span from utilities like SkePU-aware I/O routines
and time measurement via portable deterministic parallel pseudorandom
number generation to basic linear algebra and deep learning
functionality, which interface with SkePU data-containers and may
internally use SkePU skeletons to portably parallelize their
computations. Each SkePU standard library module comes with its own
namespace.

| Module | Header | Namespace |
|---|---|---|
| Pseudorandom numbers | `<skepu>` | `skepu` |
| Utility functions | `<skepu-lib/util.hpp>` | `skepu::util` |
| Complex numbers | `<skepu-lib/complex.hpp>` | `skepu::complex` |
| Linear algebra | `<skepu-lib/blas.hpp>` | `skepu::blas` |
| Image filtering | `<skepu-lib/filter.hpp>` | `skepu::filter` |
| Time measurement | `<skepu-lib/benchmark.hpp>` | `skepu::benchmark` |
| Data-container I/O | `<skepu-lib/io.hpp>` | `skepu::io` |
| Deep neural networks | `<skepu-lib/ml.hpp>` | `skepu::dnn` |
| Command line arguments | `<skepu-lib/args.hpp>` | `skepu::args` |

## Deterministic Portable Pseudorandom Number Generation

A `skepu::PRNG` is a stream of pseudorandom numbers that is attached to a skeleton instance
with `setPRNG`. A user function of `Map` (and the other skeletons that accept it, see
@tbl-featuretable) receives it as a proxy parameter `skepu::Random<N> &`, where `N` is the
number of random numbers the call draws at most, and draws from it with `get()` (an integer)
or `getNormalized()` (a floating-point number in the unit interval):

```cpp
float random_class(skepu::Random<1> &rand, int classes)
{
    return (int)(rand.getNormalized() * classes);
}

auto generate = skepu::Map<0>(random_class);
skepu::PRNG prng(0);          // the seed
generate.setPRNG(prng);
generate(labels, 10);
```

The random numbers are a function of the seed and the position of the element, not of how
the work is divided, so the CPU, OpenMP and OpenCL backends produce the same numbers
(`examples/dnn/dnn_artificial.cpp` generates its whole data set this way, and `examples/coulombic.cpp`
its atoms).

## Utility Functions

`skepu::util` has ready-made user functions for the usual arithmetic and comparisons, to use
instead of writing them for each skeleton: `identity`, `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `reciprocal`,
`negate`, `increment`, `decrement`, `square`, `min` and `max`; for example
`skepu::Map(skepu::util::square<float>)`. The binary functions also come in a form with
operands of different types.

## Complex Numbers

`skepu::complex::complex<T>` is a complex number type that is usable in user functions on all
backends, with the aliases `FComplex` (single precision) and `DComplex` (double precision) and the
arithmetic as functions (`add`, `sub`, `mul`, `real_div`, `conj`, ...) that can be used as
operators of skeletons.

## Linear Algebra

The `skepu::blas` module for basic linear algebra subroutines is described in
@sec-skepublas.

## Image Filtering and Parsing/Serialization

`skepu::filter` has pixel types (`GrayscalePixel`, `RGBPixel`, `RGBAPixel`, `HSVPixel`, ...) and
the user functions to work with them: conversions between RGB(A) and HSV(A), gamma expansion
and compression, extraction and composition of color channels and the intensity of a pixel. They
are meant as user functions for `Map` and `MapOverlap` over a `skepu::Matrix` of pixels. The
examples `edgedetect`, `image_manip` and `median` in `examples/` use them.

## Command Line Arguments

`skepu::args::Parser` reads the command line of a program: positional arguments, named options and flags, and the
backend, which nearly every SkePU program takes. A declaration returns the value at once:

```cpp
skepu::args::Parser args(argc, argv, "Perlin noise textures");   // the description is printed by --help

size_t height    = args.get<size_t>("height");                   // a positional argument, required
float persistence = args.get<float>("persistence", 0.5f);        // with a default value: optional
auto frames      = args.named<size_t>("frames", 0, "the number of frames"); // --frames 6 or --frames=6
bool adam        = args.flag("adam", "use the Adam optimizer");  // --adam

skepu::BackendSpec spec = args.backend();   // a positional argument or --backend NAME (-b NAME); set as the global backend
```

Several positional arguments can be declared at once, for structured bindings:
`auto [rows, cols] = args.get<size_t, size_t>("rows", "cols");`. The positional arguments come first on the command
line and the options after them. A value is read completely or it is an error (`abc` is not read as 0).
A name that is declared again is the same argument, and gives the value that was read the first time (also after
`backend()`), so that a function can take the parser and read the arguments it needs; another type or default value for
the name is an error.

The parser ends the program when the command line is wrong, with a message and the usage, which is made from the
declarations, and exits with status 1; `--help` prints the usage and exits with status 0. The unknown options and
arguments too many are found when the declarations are complete, which is at `backend()` (so it should be the last
declaration), at `done()` for a program without a backend, or, as a last resort, when the parser is destroyed. The
messages are printed by the first process of an MPI program only.

## Time Measurement Utilities

`skepu::benchmark` measures the execution time of skeleton calls on one or all backends.
`measure` times one call of a function (`measureExecTime` is its older name), `measureMedian` returns the median of
several calls of the function, and `basicBenchmark` returns the median of
several repetitions (as a `std::chrono::microseconds` duration); `fullBenchmark` runs a function over a range of problem sizes
for every available backend of a tuple of skeleton instances and returns a `BenchmarkResult`
with the times for each backend and size.

## Consistent Data-Container Input/Output

`skepu::io::cout` and `skepu::io::cin` are stream wrappers that print and read SkePU
containers (`Vector`, `Matrix`, tensors) and scalars consistently: the container is made
up to date on the host first (as with `skepu::external`, see @sec-external), and the access is
recorded in the trace when tracing is enabled, so that SkeVU shows it as an event. Other values
are forwarded to the underlying `std::ostream`/`std::istream`.

```cpp
skepu::io::cout << result << "\n";
```

## Convolutional and Deep Neural Network Learning and Inference

`<skepu-lib/ml.hpp>` is *SkePU-DNN*, a library for neural networks in which every layer, activation,
loss and optimizer step is computed by SkePU skeletons, so that a model trains and predicts
on every backend, including the GPUs. A model is a `skepu::dnn::SequentialModel`, built from its input dimensions (batch, and the
extents of one sample) and a chain of layers, then configured with a loss function and an
optimizer and trained on host tensors:

```cpp
using namespace skepu::dnn;

auto model = SequentialModel(Dimensions{batch_size, 28, 28, 1})
    << Conv2D(8).kernel(3, 3).weights(Init::He_uniform).biases(Init::Zero).activation(Act::ReLU)
    << MaxPooling2D().kernel(2, 2)
    << Flatten()
    << Dense(10).weights(Init::Xavier_uniform).biases(Init::Zero).activation(Act::SoftMax);

model.init();
model.configure(Loss::CategoricalCrossEntropy, Opt::Adam);
model.fit(train_x, train_y, epochs, learning_rate);        // skepu::Tensor4<float> data
auto score = model.evaluate(test_x, test_y);               // (loss, accuracy)
```

The layers are `Dense`, `Conv2D`, `Conv1D`, `MaxPooling2D`, `AvgPooling2D`, `MaxPooling1D`,
`AvgPooling1D`, `Flatten` and `Dropout`; the activations `ReLU`, `LeakyReLU`, `ELU`, `Sigmoid`,
`TanH` and `SoftMax`; the losses categorical and binary cross-entropy; the optimizers SGD and Adam.
The convolution and pooling layers support unit stride (pooling: stride equal to the pool size)
and "valid" mode; other settings are rejected with an error. `evaluate` gives the loss and accuracy of a data set (optionally with a confusion matrix),
`predict` the predictions, and `save` and `load_model` write and read a model, with its
weights, as a plain-text file (`examples/dnn/models/`).

The labels of a classification are the `n x 1 x 1 x C` tensors of one-hot vectors that the models
are trained on. `skepu::dnn::one_hot(classes, C)` makes them from a vector (or tensor) of class
numbers, `one_hot(labels, classes)` fills a tensor that is there (from the first `n` classes), and
`argmax(scores)` is the inverse: a `skepu::Vector<int>` with the class of each sample, the first of
its largest scores. They are skeleton calls, so they run on all backends and the host does not touch the
elements, and `one_hot` stops with an error if a class is not an integer from `0` to `C - 1`.

Because the tensors are ordinary SkePU data-containers and every step of a model is a skeleton call, a
network combines with other SkePU code ("DNN+X" programs): the pre- and post-processing of the data
runs on the same containers, on the same backends and without copies to the host in between. In
`examples/dnn/dnn_cifar10.cpp` the images are standardized per channel by a `MapReduce` and a `Map`, and with
`--gray` converted to grayscale by a `MapPool` before the network is trained on them; `dnn_binary.cpp` counts and
filters the classes of a data set, and `dnn_signals1d.cpp` generates its data with `skepu::randomize` and a `Map`.

The preparation of a data set is covered by skeleton calls too: `take(images, n)` (the first `n` samples),
`as_sequence(images, n)` (images as sequences for the 1D layers), `chw_to_hwc(images)` (the channels-first layout of
many data sources to that of the layers), and `channel_stats(images)` with `standardize(images, stats)` for the
per-channel normalization. The statistics are results of reductions, so every process of an MPI program has them.

Examples, using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 data
sets and synthetic data, are `examples/dnn/dnn_mnist10.cpp`, `dnn_binary.cpp`, `dnn_cifar10.cpp`, `dnn_signals1d.cpp`,
`dnn_artificial.cpp` and `dnn_model_file.cpp`.

[^13]: This is not a formal standard as decided by a standardization
    organization, but just the SkePU equivalent of the standard library
    in other programming languages.
